sources.title: Introduction to Portfolio Construction and Analysis with Python — Module 1: Analysing returns
sources.access_method: English transcripts read in the authorized Coursera browser session; supplied lab_101–lab_106 notebooks inspected locally.
sources.reuse: Original Thai teaching explanations and new hypothetical worked examples; transcripts, videos, source notebooks and course market data are not redistributed.

examples: Original hypothetical examples; no market data. Prices in THB, returns in decimal unless labelled percent. No external cash flows, fees or taxes unless explicitly discussed.
editorial_checks: Compounding simple returns and summing log returns are equivalent after conversion.
Log conversion does not remove economic losses or establish Normality or backtest quality.
Exponentiating a log return produces gross return; subtract one for simple return.
The Simon Leung 100 to 120 example has exactly 20% cumulative return.
KS tests with fitted parameters require appropriate calibration.

central_example.format: Worked lesson, optional inline Python examples and self-check questions; no separate Returns Notebook

visuals.data: Hypothetical observations at t=0, 1, 2 years; THB 1,000,000 initial wealth and simple returns +100%, -50%. Zero-baseline wealth bars; log bars use a symmetric scale about zero.
visuals.rounding: Unrounded calculations; display logs to four decimals in the lab and six in the table.
visuals.fonts: Existing locally bundled Roboto and Noto Sans Thai, embedded unchanged in SVGs.

module1_extension.reading_route: Returns contains compounding, volatility, Sharpe and drawdown. The detailed distribution, downside and VaR/ES lessons are consolidated in extreme-risk.md; original source coverage and conventions below remain recorded for the combined sequence.
module1_extension.python_examples: Inline executable examples, using pandas; no external market files required.
conventions: Sample volatility uses ddof=1, with annual scaling described as conditional on its assumptions.
Conventional Sharpe uses arithmetic excess returns; the course geometric-return convention is labelled separately.
Drawdown includes initial capital and is not annualized.
Negative skewness does not determine the proportion of observations below the mean.
High Jarque–Bera p-value does not prove Normality or independence.
Original-lab negative-subset SD, course correction mean-centered semideviation, and target downside deviation have distinct definitions.
Historical VaR uses the inverse empirical CDF of losses; ES uses exactly the stated worst-tail probability mass.
Historical methods still assume the sample is informative about the risk being estimated; Cornish–Fisher is an approximation.
